1:
Calvin turns the exhortation on a builder's image and presses it hard. By first principles he understands the rudiments taught to the ignorant when they are received into the church, and he insists that leaving them does not mean forgetting them but not remaining in them; for in building a house the foundation is never left, yet to be always engaged in laying it would be ridiculous, since whoever never proceeds to the superstructure wearies himself with useless labour. Ellicott urges the same movement out of the Greek, correcting the received rendering to the doctrine of the first principles, giving the margin's literal sense as the word of the beginning, and preferring let us press onwards, since there is an urgency the ordinary rendering misses; he notes that the word for perfection answers to the one rendered full grown just before and expresses maturity. Chrysostom does something none of the others do and turns the rebuke on his own congregation, saying he fears the same charge might fitly be made of them, that when for the time they ought to be teachers they do not even maintain the rank of learners, and that the want of attention in the taught prevents a teacher going on to higher things.

Why baptisms should be plural is the chapter's first crux, and six answers stand. Barnes finds two whose necessity Christianity teaches, by water and by the Holy Ghost, the first an emblem of the second. Gill runs through the possibilities — a change of number, the different persons and times, the threefold immersion, the threefold baptism of spirit, blood and water, the inward set beside the outward — judges none of them solid since there is but one baptism, and settles on the divers washings among the Jews. Robertson reaches the same place by authority, quoting the judgement that the plural by itself never means specifically Christian baptism either here or elsewhere but ablutions such as the mystery religions and the Jewish cultus required. Ellicott considers and rejects the rendering baptisms of teaching, on the ground that teaching would be the point of resemblance between the Jewish and Christian rites rather than the point of contrast, and explains the presence of the word doctrine as guarding against the impression that the repetition of a rite is meant. Calvin reads the two middle clauses as a parenthesis in apposition to the rest, rejects Chrysostom's account of the plural, and takes it of the solemn rites or the stated days of baptizing.

Clarke handles the same question by quoting a great predecessor at length and then declining to follow him. He gives Owen's argument in full, that doctrine is itself called baptism, that John's baptism was his doctrine and Christ's the doctrine wherewith he should sprinkle many nations, so that the two gospel baptisms are its teaching and the gifts of the Spirit, the latter being what the laying on of hands intends; and then Clarke says plainly that he is afraid, with all this great man's learning, he has not hit the apostle's meaning, since teaching is the means by which the gifts are obtained and the apostle never designed to separate them. Robertson admits that the laying on of hands seems to us out of place among elementary principles, and lists the occasions on which it served as a sign, of blessing, of healing, in the choice of the Seven, in the bestowal of the Spirit, in separation for a task and in ordination. On the closing qualification the three readings differ in temper: Barnes takes it as a simple recognition of dependence, Robertson insists it is no idle form but a real condition, and Calvin hears a dreadful denunciation, since there will not always be opportunity for making progress.
4:
How far the described experiences reach is disputed before the warning itself is reached. Robertson takes them at face value, calling them all actual spiritual experiences and noting that the adverb means once for all rather than once upon a time. Barnes says the language about tasting the good word cannot be applied to an impenitent sinner, who has no relish for the truth and sees no beauty in it, so that only a true Christian can be said to taste and enjoy it. Wesley draws the sequence out as a birth: every child naturally born first sees the light, then tastes nourishment, then partakes of the things of this world, and one born of the Spirit is described in just those three stages. Ellicott reorganises the clauses grammatically, arguing that enlightened is not the first term of a series but the thing the following clauses explain, so that the sentence runs those once enlightened, having both tasted and been made partakers and tasted. Clarke by contrast narrows the reference sharply before explaining any term: the words have no reference to any person professing Christianity, do not belong to backsliders of any kind, and apply only to apostates who reject the whole Christian system and join the blaspheming Jews in calling Christ an impostor.

The conditional in the received rendering is agreed to be wrong and disputed as to why. Clarke quotes Macknight at length: the earlier participles are aorists and were properly put in past time, so the one here should have been too, but the translators followed Beza, who without authority from any ancient manuscript inserted the word if, that the text might not appear to contradict the perseverance of the saints. Clarke adds that Macknight was himself a Calvinist and a thorough scholar who consulted candour rather than his creed. Ellicott agrees the ordinary translation is altogether incorrect, the Greek admitting one rendering only, but rejects the explanation: the suspicion that the translators were misled by dogmatic bias seems altogether unfounded, since tracing the version back finds it due not to the Genevan versions where Calvin's and Beza's influence was predominant, but to Erasmus, Luther and Tyndale. Barnes concedes on the authority of another that there is no if in the Greek, yet defends the common version as not improperly expressing the sense, treating the whole as a supposed case that may never occur, like saying that had a man fallen down a precipice it would be impossible to save him. Wesley denies exactly this: here is not a supposition but a plain relation of fact.

Calvin approaches the word impossible through its history of abuse. The passage led many to repudiate the epistle, he says, because the Novatians armed themselves with it to deny pardon to the fallen, and the Western churches refused its authority rather than refute them. He then rejects two evasions: that impossible means rare or difficult, which is wholly different from its meaning, and that the repentance meant is only the discipline preparing catechumens for baptism, since to deny that an appendage of baptism could be repeated would carry no weight against the secure. Robertson is equally unwilling to soften it, saying the infinitive with that adjective bluntly denies the possibility of renewal for apostates, that it is a terrible picture which cannot be toned down, and that the one ray of light comes later and not here. He corrects the familiar rendering of the reason, since the prefix in the verb for crucifying does not mean again or afresh but up, against the Vulgate. Calvin defends the severity as just, since the man suffers only the punishment of his own defection, and repentance is required which one wholly fallen from the gospel never truly feels. Gill, alone of them, holds the case cannot be supposed of true believers, who are held by a threefold cord.
7:
Calvin reads the similitude as an argument about timing rather than about soil. As the earth cannot bring a good crop at harvest unless it causes the seed to germinate as soon as it is sown, so if we mean to bring forth fruit the word must strike root without delay the moment the Lord sows it, since seed choked or perished cannot fructify; and the ground which sucks in the rain and at once produces a blade suitable to what was sown will by God's blessing go on to a ripe crop. Ellicott sharpens the picture climatically: land which not only receives but drinks in abundant rain must, in the climate in view, either bring forth herbage or be condemned as irretrievably barren, and the clause about tilling is added precisely to show that nothing was wanting on the part of the owner or of those who worked it. He corrects two renderings in passing, giving for whom it is also tilled rather than by whom it is dressed, and taking the blessing received as a share in what God pronounces on the fruitful earth. Robertson notes that the word for herbs is a green plant from the verb to feed, and Barnes that drinking in distinguishes mellow soil from rock where the rain runs off.

On the burning the two who reach for classical parallels reach opposite conclusions. Barnes says the allusion is to the common practice among Oriental and Roman farmers of burning bad and barren lands, and cites Pliny for it. Clarke quotes the Georgics on the same custom, with Dryden's rendering about kindled fires burning the barren ground and the light stubble crackling in the wind, and then denies that this is what is meant: the nature of the case prevents us from supposing an allusion to burning for further fertilisation, and what is described is land given up as unimprovable, its brushwood burnt off and the ground left to be pastured by the beasts. Ellicott looks to a different text altogether, finding the explanation of the last words in the description of the land God overthrew, which is brimstone and salt and burning; he adds the botanical detail that the presence of caltrops is sure evidence of a poor soil on which labour will be wasted, and notes the phrase is partly a quotation from the curse in Genesis. Robertson supplies a military note, that Roman soldiers scattered spiked balls named from the same word to hinder cavalry, and glosses the closing phrase simply as for burning, a common sight in clearing ground.

That the curse is called near rather than present is taken by two of them as the one gleam in the passage. Ellicott says that in the case of the apostates described man is helpless and God's curse is near, and then cites Chrysostom for the observation that in this very word there is mercy, since the end is not yet come. Barnes reads the same clause as devoting to destruction in the farmer's sense rather than the profane one, the land being abandoned as valueless and given over to fire. Chrysostom himself puts the emphasis on how the passage should be heard: let us hear the oracles of God with fear and much trembling, since if even our joy ought to be with trembling, what punishment do we deserve for not listening with terror to words themselves so fearful; and he insists that this threat is not the apostle's and these words are not of man but of the Holy Ghost. Gill applies the two soils allegorically throughout, the fruitful ground being those who receive the seed of the word and the thorns and briers standing for errors, heresies and evil works, which show that the seed was never sown in such hearts at all.
9:
The turn from threat to encouragement is noticed by all of them and justified by Calvin as a rule of teaching. The preceding sentences were like thunderbolts by which readers might have been struck dead, so the severity needed mitigating; and whoever wishes to do good by teaching ought so to treat his disciples as to add encouragement rather than diminish it, since nothing alienates us from the truth so much as seeing that we are deemed past hope. From this Calvin draws a conclusion running the other way too, that not only the reprobate but the elect need reproving severely. Henry sets the two appeals side by side, that having applied himself to their fears in order to prevent apostasy the writer now applies himself to their hopes, and adds the rule that it is our duty to hope well of those in whom nothing appears to the contrary. Barnes and Ellicott both hear the phrase as answering the parable just used: Barnes notes that the land overrun with briers was nigh to cursing while the things seen in these readers were nigh to salvation, and Ellicott says the writer has not written in despair but for warning only, believing that what borders on them is not the curse but the alternative.

That God would be unrighteous to forget their work raises the question of merit, and Calvin meets it head on. The words seem to make God a debtor to human service, and the schoolmen made much of the sentence, concluding that it would be unjust for him not to render eternal salvation as the reward of works; his reply is that the apostle is not here speaking of the cause of our salvation, so that no opinion about the merit of works can be formed from the passage. Clarke reaches a similar place by a different route, holding that God is bound to men only by his own promise, which he was not obliged to make, but that once made his justice requires him to keep it — so that, in his phrase, God's promise is God's debt. Ellicott states the same distinction in one line, that man's work cannot in itself merit reward from God but the righteous God cannot neglect his own promise and law that such works shall receive reward. Barnes gives two reasons why forgetting would be unrighteous, that it was fitting the work be remembered and that reward was expressly promised. Robertson adds a dry qualification that limits the whole: even God cannot remember what they did not do.

Two of them agree on a textual point and neither cites the other. Clarke reports that the word for labour before love is wanting in almost every manuscript and version of importance and that Griesbach left it out of the text; Ellicott says the best manuscripts omit it, so that the clause should run to forget your work, and the love which ye showed toward his name. Robertson notices a difference of tense in the next clause, the same verb appearing first as an aorist and then a present, single act against repeated acts, which the received rendering catches with ministered and still do minister. On the closing exhortation, Ellicott prefers become not sluggish and points out that the adjective is the one used earlier of their dullness in apprehending truth, now applied to hope and life; Robertson agrees and notes that some were already such. Ellicott distinguishes the word for patience here from the one used later in the epistle, that being brave endurance and this the term usually rendered long-suffering, which here signifies patient waiting. Calvin explains why one example is singled out from the many who shared the same faith, since a naked truth does not affect us as much as seeing what is required of us fulfilled in a particular person.
13:
Chrysostom explains the strategy of the appeal before its substance. Having boldly reflected on their faults and sufficiently alarmed them, the writer consoles them first by praises and then, on stronger ground, by the assurance that they will attain what they hope for; and he draws that consolation not from things future but from things past, which will the rather persuade them, since in the matter of punishment he alarms by what is to come and in the matter of prizes he encourages by what has been. From this Chrysostom infers a divine habit: not to bring in what has been promised immediately but after a long time, both to present the greatest proof of his power and to lead us to faith, so that those living in tribulation without having received the promises may not faint. Ellicott states the connection as a parallel drawn for the readers, that they like Abraham have promises to which God has given all possible certainty and can attain the fulfilment only through faith and patient waiting. Both he and Barnes explain why this example rather than another: Barnes because Abraham relied on a promise when appearances were against its fulfilment and so shows the advantage of perseverance, Ellicott because the assurance given him was confirmed by oath and because it included the promise of the Christ.

On the oath the commentators are brief and agreed. Barnes states the ground flatly, that there is no being greater than God. Clarke fills in what the pledge amounted to, that God pledged his eternal power and Godhead for the fulfilment of the promise, there being no superior to whom he could appeal or by whom he could be bound, so that he appeals to and pledges his own immutable truth. Clarke also supplies the occasion, that the promise referred to was made when Abraham had offered his son on the altar, and quotes the passage in full, that in blessing God would bless him and multiply his seed as the stars of heaven and the sand upon the seashore, and that in his seed all the nations of the earth should be blessed; the apostle quotes only a part, as is generally the case, because he knew his readers were well acquainted with the older Scriptures. Ellicott adds that although the words are taken from the account of the offering, the writer probably has earlier promises in mind as well, and that the promises made to Abraham were essentially one, with various parts progressively fulfilled. Robertson notes only the tenses of the two verbs for swearing.

What Abraham actually obtained is where they divide. Calvin and Barnes take it of the numerous posterity, and both dwell on the delay. Calvin sets out the improbability: Sarah had been barren through life, both had reached a sterile old age and were nearer the grave than the marriage bed, and who could believe a nation equalling the stars in number would proceed from them, a thing contrary to all reason; yet Abraham looked for it and feared no disappointment because he relied on the word, and after waiting twenty-five years a son was given. Barnes counts the interval differently, noting that Abraham was seventy-five when called, that twenty-four years passed before the manner of the fulfilment was made known, and that he was a hundred before it held good. Clarke extends the obtaining forward instead, holding that the supernatural birth of Isaac only began the fulfilment, that Abraham saw provision made for the multiplying of his seed, and that continuing steadfast he received the end of all the promises in the enjoyment of an eternal glory. Ellicott denies exactly this reading of the verse: though some portions of the promise received a partial accomplishment during Abraham's life, it is not that which the writer has in view.
16:
Calvin reads the oath as an accommodation and then turns it into an argument for assurance. God as a gracious Father accommodates himself to our slowness to believe, and seeing that we do not rest on his simple word he adds an oath to impress it more fully; from which Calvin infers how much it concerns us to know that there is such certainty about his goodwill that no occasion for wavering remains. He presses the inference from God's own law about swearing: since God forbids his name to be taken on a slight occasion and threatens vengeance on those who abuse it, he holds that name in the highest honour, so that one who forbids men to swear without reason and has yet been pleased to swear himself shows how necessary the certainty of salvation is. Ellicott brings out the oddity of the construction, that when a man confirms a promise by solemn appeal to God, God stands as mediator between the two; here God, condescending to human weakness, is at once the promiser and the mediator, so that God the promiser appeals to God the hearer and witness. Robertson notes the verb is used elsewhere of acting as surety.

What the two immutable things are is disputed, and Barnes reports the alternatives before choosing. Most expositors, he says, naming Doddridge, Whitby, Rosenmuller, Koppe and Calvin, take them for the promise and the oath, each a firm ground of assurance in which it would be impossible for God to lie; but one commentator refers them instead to two oaths, the one sworn to Abraham and the one by which the Messiah was made high priest after the order of Melchisedec. Barnes objects that the apostle seems to refer to two things distinct in their nature rather than to two acts of the same kind. Clarke, Ellicott, Robertson and Calvin all take the ordinary view, Clarke distinguishing what each pledges, the promise pledging faithfulness and justice and the oath all the infinite perfections of the Godhead. Clarke also quotes a rabbinic saying on by thine own self: had God sworn by heaven and earth, one might say that as these pass away so might the oath, but having sworn by his great name which endures for ever, his oath endures for ever. Calvin makes the same point in his own terms, that the word of God is in itself worthy of trust, so that when an oath is added it is an overplus added to a full measure.

The anchor draws out the most sustained imagery in the chapter, and each of them develops it differently. Clarke builds a scene: a vessel nearing port cannot get in over shallow and broken water, so she carries her sheet anchor inside the pier head by means of her boat and rides out the storm at the length of her cable, agitated but not driving, until the tide flows and the crew wear her in against the anchor that has kept its hold. Calvin presses the comparison and then notes where it fails: as long as we sojourn here we stand on no firm ground but are tossed as in a turbulent sea, and the anchor cast through the water into a dark unseen place keeps the beaten vessel from being overwhelmed — but the anchor is cast downwards, having the earth for its bottom, whereas our hope rises upwards and soars aloft, finding nothing in the world to stand on. Barnes quotes Socrates twice, that grounding hope on a false supposition is like trusting to a weak anchor, and that a ship ought not to trust one anchor nor life one hope. Ellicott notes the symbol is absent from the older Scriptures but current in Greek proverbs and found on ancient coins. Robertson observes that the anchor is out of sight but holds, which is what matters.
